lessonPlan.title: The Story of an Hour unit
lessonPlan.author: Kate Chopin
lessonPlan.editionNote: Reading text: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Story_of_an_Hour (revision 13961357), cleaned for Liber et Libri.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 9–12 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Story of an Hour.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Story of an Hour: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Short story: read whole in one 90-minute lesson (assign longer stories as pre-reading). Middle School prompts use the full text when the grade tags include 6–8; otherwise teacher-selected passages.
lessonPlan.schedule: One 90-minute lesson (the whole story), with an optional take-home essay
essentialQuestions: What does The Story of an Hour suggest about freedom and marriage?
What does The Story of an Hour suggest about identity?
What does The Story of an Hour suggest about irony of joy?
objectives: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly and implicitly.
Determine themes and analyze their development over the course of the story.
Analyze how characters, setting and point of view interact.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.

Each prompt is tagged for Common Core, Indiana 2023, Dual Credit (Indiana College Core), AP and Cambridge where they apply.

Writing prompt at assigned rigor (one graded per week)

wholeBookTest.title: The Story of an Hour: whole-book test

items.prompt: Why is Mrs. Mallard told the news carefully?
What does she see from her window?
options: Signs of spring and new life

items.prompt: What do the doctors say killed her?
options: Heart disease, the joy that kills

items.prompt: In the line “She did not know; it was too subtle and elusive to name.”, what does “elusive” most nearly mean?
options: hard to grasp, catch or put into words
in a self-collected or self-possessed manner
having the capacity for thought and reason especially to a high degree

items.prompt: In the line “Her pulses beat fast, and the coursing blood warmed and relaxed every inch of her body.”, what does “coursing” most nearly mean?
options: in a self-collected or self-possessed manner
having the capacity for thought and reason especially to a high degree
hard to grasp, catch or put into words

items.prompt: As used in the story (“She did not know; it was too subtle and elusive to name.”), what does “elusive” mean?
options: hard to grasp, catch or put into words
the holding back of feelings or desires
continuing firmly in spite of difficulty

items.prompt: As used in the story (“Her pulses beat fast, and the coursing blood warmed and relaxed every inch of her body.”), what does “coursing” mean?
options: in a wild, stormy, excited way
in a self-collected or self-possessed manner

items.prompt: As used in the story (“It was Brently Mallard who entered, a little travel-stained, composedly carrying his grip-sack and umbrella.”), what does “composedly” mean?
options: a pause in which something is held off or stopped
sudden understanding; a flash of insight
in a self-collected or self-possessed manner
having the capacity for thought and reason especially to a high degree

items.prompt: As used in the story (“It was not a glance of reflection, but rather indicated a suspension of intelligent thought.”), what does “intelligent” mean?
options: continuing firmly in spite of difficulty
hard to grasp, catch or put into words
the holding back of feelings or desires
having the capacity for thought and reason especially to a high degree

items.prompt: As used in the story (“She was young, with a fair, calm face, whose lines bespoke repression and even a certain strength.”), what does “repression” mean?
options: the holding back of feelings or desires
in a wild, stormy, excited way

shortAnswer: Explain how freedom and marriage develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how identity develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how irony of joy develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (freedom and marriage, identity, irony of joy) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what The Story of an Hour teaches about freedom and marriage. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Kate Chopin develops freedom and marriage in The Story of an Hour. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Kate Chopin develops freedom and marriage across The Story of an Hour. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of The Story of an Hour (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of freedom and marriage. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of freedom and marriage in The Story of an Hour. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Kate Chopin's choices in The Story of an Hour (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of freedom and marriage, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places The Story of an Hour's treatment of freedom and marriage in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on freedom and marriage in The Story of an Hour that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on freedom and marriage in The Story of an Hour. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about freedom and marriage in The Story of an Hour, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on freedom and marriage in The Story of an Hour, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
